# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Contemporary Narrative Review

## Introduction and epidemiology

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein as amyloid fibrils within the myocardium, producing progressive ventricular wall thickening, restrictive physiology, and ultimately heart failure [1]. Molecular mechanisms of amyloidosis were defined by Merlini and Bellotti, who established that diverse precursor proteins share a common pathway of misfolding and aggregation [2]. More than 95% of clinically relevant cases arise from two precursors: immunoglobulin light chain (AL) amyloidosis and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis, the latter occurring in hereditary (ATTRv) and wild-type (ATTRwt) forms [3]. Long regarded as rare, CA is now recognised as substantially underdiagnosed. In a landmark prospective study, among elderly patients admitted with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and left ventricular hypertrophy, 16 of 120 (13.3%) showed moderate-to-severe uptake on 99mTc-DPD scintigraphy, identifying ATTRwt as an important cause of HFpEF [4]. A subsequent meta-analysis confirmed ATTR-CM in roughly 12% of HFpEF patients and in a comparable proportion of elderly patients with severe aortic stenosis [5].

## Pathophysiology

In AL amyloidosis, a small, often indolent plasma-cell clone produces misfolded free light chains. Systemic amyloidosis is caused by misfolding and extracellular deposition of circulating proteins as amyloid fibrils, resulting in the dysfunction of vital organs; the most common form, AL amyloidosis, is caused by misfolded light chains produced by a small, dangerous B-cell clone [6]. Beyond mechanical infiltration, circulating light chains exert direct cardiotoxic effects, which accounts for the disproportionately severe and rapidly progressive cardiac dysfunction characteristic of AL disease [7]. Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy is caused by the deposition of transthyretin amyloid fibrils in the myocardium; the deposition occurs when wild-type or variant transthyretin becomes unstable and misfolds [8]. Tetramer dissociation into monomers is the rate-limiting step in ATTR amyloidogenesis, providing the rationale for stabiliser therapy.

## Clinical recognition and diagnosis

CA should be suspected in patients with unexplained ventricular hypertrophy, HFpEF, low-voltage ECG with increased wall thickness, or associated "red flags" such as carpal tunnel syndrome. The 2021 ESC position statement notes that the majority of cases (>98%) are related to monoclonal light chain or transthyretin deposition, ATTR amyloidosis can be hereditary or acquired/wild-type, and screening can be considered when left ventricular wall thickness is ≥12 mm with additional suggestive findings [9]. The diagnostic paradigm was transformed by the demonstration that bone-avid radiotracer scintigraphy can confirm ATTR non-invasively. In a multicentre study, myocardial radiotracer uptake on bone scintigraphy was >99% sensitive and 86% specific for cardiac ATTR amyloid, with false positives almost exclusively reflecting unrecognised AL disease [10]. Consequently, cardiac scintigraphy can confirm the diagnosis of ATTR-CM only when combined with blood and urine testing to exclude a monoclonal protein [11]. Free light chain assay with serum and urine immunofixation is therefore mandatory, and any patient with a positive monoclonal screen requires tissue biopsy and amyloid typing [1].

Multimodality imaging complements scintigraphy. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance with T1 mapping quantifies expanded extracellular volume (ECV); extracellular deposition of amyloid fibrils within the myocardium significantly expands the ECV, and affected patients develop severe heart failure and face a dismal prognosis [12]. In AL amyloidosis, native T1 and ECV provide both diagnostic and prognostic value [13]. Genetic sequencing of the TTR gene is required in all confirmed ATTR patients to distinguish hereditary from wild-type disease [1].

## Prognosis and staging

Biomarker-based staging guides management. A novel staging system based on cardiac biomarkers was developed by Grogan and colleagues to determine the natural history of ATTRwt and predictors of survival [14]. The widely used staging score developed in 2018 by Gillmore et al. stratifies patients with ATTR-CA into prognostic categories based on NT-proBNP levels and eGFR, with NT-proBNP ≤3000 ng/L and eGFR ≥45 mL/min classified as Stage I and the converse as Stage III [15]. For AL amyloidosis, effective regimens have markedly improved survival, but the 25% to 30% early death rate has not changed, with patients dying within weeks of cardiac failure due to late diagnosis [16].

## Treatment

The therapeutic landscape has been revolutionised. For AL amyloidosis, the ANDROMEDA trial established that the addition of subcutaneous daratumumab to bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone resulted in significantly better outcomes in newly diagnosed patients [17], confirmed by long-term overall survival and organ-response benefit [18].

For ATTR-CM, tafamidis, a TTR stabiliser, was the first disease-modifying therapy: in the ATTR-ACT trial it reduced all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalisations [19], and tafamidis binds to transthyretin, preventing tetramer dissociation and amyloidogenesis [8]. Acoramidis, a high-affinity stabiliser, subsequently demonstrated efficacy: it inhibits dissociation of tetrameric TTR and leads to more than 90% stabilization across the dosing interval, improving the hierarchical clinical outcome in ATTRibute-CM [20]. Gene-silencing approaches reduce hepatic TTR production. Patisiran, an RNA-interference therapeutic, improved neuropathy and showed favourable cardiac effects in hereditary ATTR [21,22], and CMR studies have shown reduction in CMR-derived extracellular volume with patisiran indicates cardiac amyloid regression [23]. The HELIOS-B trial then established subcutaneous vutrisiran in ATTR-CM, where in patients with ATTR-CM, who have high mortality and morbidity, vutrisiran reduced the composite of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events [24]. Real-world cohorts corroborate the survival benefit of stabiliser therapy [25,26].

## Conclusion

CA has shifted from an untreatable rarity to a recognised, stageable, and increasingly treatable cause of heart failure [27,28]. Non-invasive diagnosis, biomarker staging, and a growing armamentarium of stabilisers, silencers, and plasma-cell–directed therapy now make early recognition imperative [29,30].
